stories.headline: Ukraine's mass drone attack on the Moscow region kills two as Russia's parliamentary election enters its final day

sources.body:
At least two people have been killed and six injured in a "massive" overnight Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, Governor Andrei Vorobyev has said.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones heading for the capital had been shot down in what he called an "unprecedented attack". An oil refinery was damaged and several homes were set ablaze.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed Kyiv had hit a "key" Russian oil facility and a logistics site in the region, representing "billions of dollars that sustain the war machine".

Ukrainian officials meanwhile said eight people, including three children, had been killed in Russian attacks in the Kyiv and Sumy regions on Saturday.

Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.

A 44-year-old woman was killed in Sofyino on Sunday after a drone hit a three-storey residential building, regional head Vorobyev said. Another five people - including two children - were injured.

An elderly man died after a private house was hit in the Orekhovo-Zuevo district, Vorobyev added.

Videos have emerged on social media appearing to show explosions in the night skies above Moscow, and a burning warehouse. The footage has not been verified by the BBC.

Mayor Sobyanin said a drone had struck a building near one of the capital's boulevards and a facility at an oil refinery was damaged in "an attempt to disrupt" Russia's parliamentary election.

Sunday is the third day of voting in an election that is tightly controlled by the Kremlin and which critics have dismissed as neither free, fair nor transparent.

Russian state media reported that an election official was one of two people killed by a drone attack on a bus in a Moscow-controlled part of Kherson in Ukraine on Sunday, citing the head of Russia's election commission.

Meanwhile, Moscow's biggest airport Sheremetyevo warned passengers "temporary restrictions" were in place overnight, while at the capital's Vnukovo airport all arrivals and departures were halted. Restrictions at both airports were lifted by Sunday morning but each warned some flights may still be delayed.

It comes after a mother and her two small children, a boy and a girl, were killed in a Russian attack in the city of Fastiv, Kyiv on Sautrday, according to regional head Tymur Tkachenko.

He later said a child injured in a separate attack in Vyshhorod, north of Kyiv, had also died in hospital.

In the north-eastern Sumy region, four people were killed when a Russian drone hit the car they were travelling in, top local official Oleh Hryhorov said.

Both Russia and Ukraine have continued to hit energy infrastructure targets in the past week, despite US President Donald Trump claiming on social media that the two sides had agreed not to do so.

Trump signed a sanctions bill on Friday that targets Russia's economy by implementing tariffs on the biggest buyers of the country's oil and gas which include China and India.

The US legislation gives the US president powers to impose 100% tariffs on major purchasers of Russian energy.
sources.headline: Two killed in 'massive' Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow region, Russia says

sources.body:
Authorities accuse Ukraine of trying to disrupt poll and say 1,600 drones in total intercepted, while at least two people killed and oil refinery damaged

Hundreds of drones targeting Moscow and its surrounding region killed at least two people and damaged a major refinery on the final day of the country’s parliamentary elections, authorities said on Sunday.

The capital’s mayor said that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow.

Sergei Sobyanin accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with a tightly controlled three-day election that is set to tighten president Vladimir Putin’s 26-year grip on power.

“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.

Moscow’s regional governor said at least two people were killed – a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man – in two separate locations.

A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building also led to 400 people being evacuated, said Moscow regional governor, Andrey Vorobyov, without specifying the drones’ origin.

The attacks come at a time when Kyiv stepped up its long-range drone strike campaign against Russia in recent months, particularly against energy infrastructure to target a vital source of the Kremlin’s revenue to fund its war effort – now in its fifth year.

Ukrainian ​strikes have knocked out a significant part of Russia’s oil refining capacity, triggering oil product shortages, fuel price increases and long queues at filling stations in many regions across the country’s 11 time zones.

A facility on the territory of the Moscow oil refinery had been damaged, Sobyanin said. No casualties had been reported so far and emergency services were on the scene.

That major refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.

Ukraine has not commented on the attacks. Both sides ​say they do not ‌target civilians.

The latest strike comes after the US president, Donald Trump, said on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities.

It also comes after Russians began voting on Friday in the country’s first parliamentary election since Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Only parties that support Putin and the Kremlin’s military campaign have been registered to run. Moscow has also organised voting in occupied Ukraine.

Few Russians doubt Putin’s United Russia party will coast to victory again, but the vote offers a gauge of public support for the war.
sources.headline: Hundreds of drones target Moscow on last day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary election

sources.body:
Moscow mayor says Russia intercepted 1,600 drones since Saturday, including 450 directed at the capital.

At least two people have been killed and a major refinery has been damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s capital, Moscow, and its surrounding region, as the Russian parliamentary elections enter their final day.

Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Sunday that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted and shot down, 450 of which were heading for Moscow.

Meanwhile in Ukraine, authorities said at least four people were killed in overnight Russian attacks on the Kyiv region, including three children.

The attacks come as Russia and Ukraine continue to escalate long-range strikes against each other.

Moscow regional Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on social media that a 44-year-old woman and an elderly man were killed in two separate Ukrainian attacks. A fire triggered by a drone crashing into a 21-storey building forced the evacuation of 400 people, Vorobyov said.

Sobyanin said a facility at the Moscow oil refinery was also damaged in the wave of attacks, and emergency services were on the scene. The major refinery has already been hit by Ukrainian strikes in recent months.

He accused Ukraine of attempting to interfere with Russia’s tightly controlled three-day election.

“The unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed,” he said on Telegram.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the strikes, saying: “Our long-range responses had a very significant impact in the Moscow region last night.”

“One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine,” he posted on X.

Separately, the head ⁠of ⁠Russia’s election commission said that ⁠a drone attack on ⁠a civilian bus had killed two people, including an election official, ‌in a Russian-occupied part of Kherson region in Ukraine, RIA news agency reported.

The strikes come as Kyiv has intensified its long-range drone campaign against Russia, particularly targeting energy infrastructure to cut off a vital source of Kremlin revenue used to fund its war effort, now in its fifth year.

Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvedenko, reporting from Moscow, said this was among the largest single day attacks on Russia since the war began.

“I have not seen numbers this large in the four and a half years of this conflict, especially in the past six months when Ukrainian attacks have escalated,” he said.

Medvedenko said it’s no coincidence that this large-scale attack is happening on the last day of the Russian elections.

“This is the most important final day of the election. Will it cause people to express their frustration with how this conflict has been affecting them directly after four and a half years? Will it cause them to rally around the flag here, show unity, as Vladimir Putin was calling on people to do. We will have to wait and see.”

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Air Force Command reported that Russia launched 138 drones of various types across the country overnight, according to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency. It said that air defences managed to shoot down or neutralise 101 of them.
sources.headline: Mass Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow kills two, Russia says

stories.headline: Two German state elections test Chancellor Merz as the far right seeks further gains

sources.body:
Local elections are taking place in two German states on Sunday which could increase the political pressure on Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Opinion polls in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommerm suggest Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) is at risk of damaging defeats, which would raise further questions about the chancellor's future.

These latest elections come after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won a major victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago, while the CDU saw its vote halved.

There has been speculation in Germany that Merz could be replaced as chancellor mid-term unless the CDU's political fortunes improve.

He has said he will carry on but is facing poor approval ratings amid rumours of a so-called chancellor swap, though his challengers are "still hesitating", writes German news site Tagesschau .

According to the polls, Merz's conservatives could lose power in Berlin as it tussles with Die Linke (The Left) over first place.

Meanwhile in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU has only just been hovering above the 5% threshold needed for a party to enter the state parliament. It could spell their worst ever result in a state election.

How did it come to this after just 16 months in power? Friedrich Merz is having to answer for the tumbling popularity of his own party, while the political force that he aimed to counter - the AfD - continues its rise.

Some branches of the AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects.

But its anti-immigration, Russian-friendly, Germany-first agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

The AfD is hoping to build on its recent landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt by topping the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

However, the centre-left SPD has staged a late comeback to be in contention for the top spot through its lead candidate, Manuela Schwesig.

Currently the state premier, Schwesig is trying to sweep up the anti-AfD vote as she bills herself as the "Die Frau gegen Blau" - "Woman against Blue", the AfD's party colours.

But her local popularity belies the far poorer fortunes of her national party which is locked in a loveless coalition with Merz's CDU.

In a queue for a campaign event in the city of Neubrandenburg, AfD supporter Reinhart tells us that the traditional parties are being washed away.

"Not only in Germany. In Italy, in France, in Great Britain. Everywhere the traditional parties go down."

He smiles when asked what he thinks of Merz, saying: "Oh well everyone thinks the same about him.

"He is arrogant, out of touch, not on the same level as the general public."

Merz's backers argue that the chancellor has had a tough time with global events and that a lot of the problems the nation faces are ones he has inherited.

But whatever faith people had in his ability to fix those problems, it is apparently ebbing away - and, the brutal truth is, it can be hard to find voters who like him.

The former corporate lawyer's tack to the right on issues like immigration has failed to erode AfD support while also alienating people further to the left.
sources.headline: German elections under way which could decide fate of Chancellor Merz

sources.body:
Embattled Friedrich Merz faces nervous wait while far-right Alternative für Deutschland party targets further gains

Voters in two German states are going to the polls with the political future of the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz , hanging in the balance and an emboldened far right targeting further gains.

Coming two weeks after a seismic election in Saxony-Anhalt in which the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored its highest ever result in a regional poll, the nativist party is expected to drain support again from Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Just how brutal the outcome is could affect Merz’s ability to hang on as leader after only 16 months in power, possibly setting wheels in motion for his replacement or even snap elections – currently regarded as unlikely but not ruled out.

About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the capital Berlin and nearly 1.3 million in the Baltic coast state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Polling booths open at 8am local time on Sunday and will close at 6pm, when Merz and his allies will be watching exit polls on tenterhooks.

The luckless chancellor has resisted calls to quit and vowed to fight for a signature package of economic and social welfare changes he argues are crucial to Germany’s future.

“We as a government were elected for four years, I was elected for four years,” he told an industry group. “And I want to use these four years to lead the country out of this difficult period.”

Merz, whose personal approval ratings have nosedived to 10%, cancelled a plan to speak at the UN general assembly in New York because “his presence is required in Berlin” after the elections, a government official said.

His credibility has been tarnished by broken campaign promises to return Europe’s largest economy to growth and cut the AfD, the biggest opposition party in parliament and number one in opinion polls, down to size.

The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority in former communist Saxony-Anhalt, which would have allowed it to govern on its own. It is looking for defectors from other parties to make it the first far-right force to run a German state since the Nazi period.

However, polls indicate the AfD will fall well short of such a prospect in both of Sunday’s elections, even with its palpable sense of momentum.

In Berlin, which is one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the incumbent CDU is vying for first place against the far-left Die Linke, which has called for expropriation of corporate landlords to fight rising housing costs.

About 85% of Berlin households rent their ​homes and advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014, when the city was still labelled “poor but sexy” by its then mayor, Klaus Wowereit.

The AfD is polling strongly in third or fourth place, even in the cosmopolitan capital.

The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the CDU, abandoned his re-election bid in July after getting tangled in contradictions explaining a decision to play tennis while large parts of the German capital were hit by an arson-triggered power blackout last winter.
sources.headline: Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls

sources.body:
Far-right AfD defeated German chancellor’s CDU in recent Saxony-Anhalt state election, casting doubt on his future.

Voters in the eastern German states of Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are heading to the polls as far-right and far-left gains threaten to affect the political standing of Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

About 2.5 million people are eligible to vote in the city-state of Berlin, Germany’s capital, and nearly 1.3 million in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday. Polling booths in both states – traditionally seen as left-leaning – opened at 8am local time (06:00 GMT) and will close at 6pm (16:00 GMT).

Pressure on Merz has been mounting after the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) delivered a major defeat to his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party two weeks ago in the key state of Saxony-Anhalt . The AfD fell just short of an absolute majority, which would have allowed it to govern on its own.

After just 16 months in power, Merz’s approval ratings have plunged to about 14 percent, the latest polls suggest, as he struggles to push through promised economic and social welfare reforms with his centre-left coalition partners, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), raising doubts among fellow party members about whether he can continue to lead.

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU is an onlooker to the main battle between the SPD’s popular state premier Manuela Schwesig and the AfD’s lead candidate, former radio presenter Leif-Erik Holm.

While the AfD was polling at 36 percent against the SPD’s 37 percent, Merz’s CDU, at just 6 percent, was dangerously close to the 5 percent hurdle needed to stay in the state parliament, according to public broadcaster ZDF.

Reporting from a polling station in Schwerin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said there was “very much all to play for” in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

“The race between the AfD here and the Social Democrat government is very close indeed,” he added, pointing out the recent opinion polls.

In Berlin, the CDU is running a tight race against the far-left Die Linke (The Left), which promises drastic measures to solve a dire housing crisis and is popular with young people.

Regional elections would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shockwaves through Europe.

“Saxony-Anhalt was certainly a revolution for the German party system,” Florian Hartleb, a professor of international relations at Modul University in Vienna and expert on far-right movements, told Al Jazeera.

Hartleb said the AfD had been “fundamentally excluded” from the power system, with the other political parties trying “everything” against it in recent years. “But it didn’t work out,” he said, citing voters’ dissatisfaction over migration, the economy and social inequality.

Merz has reportedly scheduled a crisis CDU meeting and cleared his calendar to deal with potential aftershocks from Sunday’s elections.
sources.headline: Two German states go to the polls after far-right gains

stories.headline: Houthis claim missile strikes on Riyadh as Saudi Arabia says its air defenses intercepted an attack

sources.body:
Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen say they carried out drone and ballistic missile attacks on the Saudi capital Riyadh, as well as energy sites on the country's Red Sea coast.

Saudi authorities said they intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired at Riyadh on Saturday, without confirming any further strikes or causalities.

Earlier, a column of black smoke was seen rising from fuel tanks near the Saudi capital's international airport, where flights were disrupted temporarily on Saturday.

Air raid alerts had sounded in the capital for the first time since the Iran-backed Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia in July.

The US state department urged Americans in the Middle East to "exercise vigilance and be prepared for potential flight cancellations and other travel disruptions".

"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including civilian airports. This military conflict has the potential to escalate rapidly," it said in a statement.

It added that Americans "should seriously reconsider travel to and through the region".

Air defences also stopped "hostile attempts to target civilians" in the cities of Bish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu, an official spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.

In a statement posted online, Houthi military spokesman Yahya al-Sarea said a "large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones" had been used to attack "sensitive sites" in Riyadh and Aramco state oil and gas company facilities in Yanbu on the coast.

He added that the attacks were "in response to the Saudi enemy's criminal attempts" to target the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which is currently controlled by the Houthis.

Earlier, Sarea had accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out 300 strikes across Yemen during the past week.

The Houthis are locked in a civil war with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

They have attacked targets inside Saudi Arabia on several occasions in recent months, and said this week that they were responsible for downing a Saudi fighter jet over Yemen.

According to an unconfirmed report from AFP news agency, quoting military sources on both sides of Yemen's civil war, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces claimed 48 lives on Saturday.

The Houthis said 31 of their fighters had been killed while government sources said their side had lost 17 soldiers, according to the news agency.

On Friday, the International Organization for Migration, a UN body, reported that the number of people displaced as a result of recent fighting had passed 104,796 .

A number of apparent explosions were heard in Riyadh and major problems were reported at King Khalid International Airport earlier on Saturday, with the tracking website FlightRadar24 reporting delays and cancellations.

An AFP journalist reported that firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank belonging to Aramco.

The Saudi Civil Defence had sent out phone alerts overnight warning of potential danger in Riyadh and other regions, before issuing an all-clear on Saturday morning.
sources.headline: Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles

sources.body:
Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July

Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday.

The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July.

Explosions were heard in Riyadh as firefighters battled to extinguish the flames of a burning fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi oil company Aramco near the city’s King Khalid international airport.

Residents told Agence France-Presse that hours after the alert, they had heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the Saudi capital.

According to tracking website FlightRadar24, there were “major problems” at the airport and it has been listed under its maximum disruption index.

“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident told AFP, speaking on condition of anonymity.

The Saudi civil defence force sent air raid alerts overnight on Friday to residents of Riyadh, Jeddah and other cities including Yanbu, a major industrial port which is home to critical oil facilities. The military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defences had destroyed a missile fired by the Yemeni group toward ​Riyadh.

The all-clear was given shortly afterwards, but residents were encouraged not to gather in crowds.

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the group had foiled unspecified “criminal attempts” ⁠in the Yemeni capital of Sana’a, blaming Saudi Arabia and vowing a response. The group also said the Saudi air force had conducted hundreds of airstrikes against it in recent days.

The UN security council condemned the continued ​Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia in a statement on Friday. It said they had included attacks that affected civilian and energy infrastructure and had injured civilians, including women and children.

It also condemned the Houthis’ military offensive in Yemen, where nearly 105,000 people have fled their homes , the International Organization for Migration said on Wednesday.

The security council’s 15 members called for “practical cooperation” to prevent the Houthis from acquiring arms, military training, financing and other military-related assistance needed to carry out their attacks. They stressed that all countries must enforce the UN arms embargo against the group.

The Houthis recently seized control of strategic the Red Sea islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish. Earlier this month, the group captured the port of Mokha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandab strait, fueling fears the world could face a second oil supply crisis.

The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has developed as a new theatre of conflict in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes against Iran at the end of February. Donald Trump has rebuffed Saudi requests for direct US military intervention against the Houthis.
sources.headline: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital

sources.body:
This was the first time an alert was sounded in Riyadh since an escalation between the Houthis in Yemen and the Saudis.

Saudi-led coalition forces fighting Yemen’s Houthis have said that the Iran-backed group fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh at dawn before it was intercepted and destroyed.

“The Houthis also attempted to target civilians and civilian infrastructure in Bisha, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu,” coalition forces spokesperson Major-General Turki al-Maliki wrote on X on Saturday, adding that the attacks were thwarted by the Gulf monarchy’s air defences.

Saudi Arabia warned of a “hostile aerial threat” and issued a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom overnight on Friday.

On Saturday, at least one explosion was heard in Riyadh, with residents near the airport saying they saw a large plume of black smoke later in the morning. Saudi authorities reported no casualties or damage.

It was the first air raid alert sounded in Riyadh since an escalation in fighting with the Houthis in Yemen began in July.

The Saudi spokesperson said that the Houthis are escalating their attempts to target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital. He also affirmed the coalition command’s right to take “appropriate” action to deter the Houthis, in accordance with international humanitarian law.

Earlier on Saturday, Houthi fighters in Yemen said they attacked “sensitive” sites in Riyadh as well as an Aramco oil facility in the western coastal city of Yanbu, according to a statement shared by Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree.

Saree said the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia with cruise and ballistic missiles as well as drones.

“You could see that the Houthis are determining the timelines and the levels of the escalation,” Yasmeen al-Eryani, executive director for knowledge production at the Sana’a Center think tank, told Al Jazeera. “So, depending on the current situation, it seems that the Houthis are the ones in control,” she added.

Meanwhile, on the ground in Yemen, the armed forces of the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government said their fighters thwarted a Houthi infiltration attempt in the al-Fuliahan sector in southern Marib on Saturday, killing 12 Houthi fighters and injuring others.

The army also said 13 Yemeni soldiers were killed in two days of clashes with Houthi forces in the southwestern provinces of Taiz and Lahj.

Renewed clashes are taking place in Yemen’s Marib, Taiz, Lahj, al-Jawf and al-Bayda as part of a military escalation that began in early July – the most intense since the relative calm following an April 2022 truce.

Al-Eryani told Al Jazeera that military options against the Houthis are currently limited because much of the fighting is taking place in mountainous terrain that is difficult for opposing forces to access and hold.

For now, she said, containing the group may be a more realistic option than defeating it militarily. “Without controlling the peaks that are parallel to the coast, you will not be able to control the coast,” said al-Eryani.
sources.headline: Saudi-led coalition says defence intercepted Houthi missile fired at Riyadh

stories.headline: DR Congo begins Ebola vaccinations for health workers as the death toll rises

sources.body:
50,000 frontline staff to receive a jab for a different Ebola strain, with 20,000 enrolled in a one-year clinical trial.

Health workers in parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have begun to receive a vaccine that many hope will provide a level of protection against the Ebola virus.

The vaccine rollout started on Saturday in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in the northeastern DRC. Ituri is the epicentre of the fastest-growing outbreak of Ebola in history.

The provincial governor, Major-General Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, said health workers there “are particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response”.

The operation, backed by the World Health Organization and Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, will also target North Kivu, where cases have been rising sharply, health authorities said.

Some 50,000 health and other frontline workers will be injected with the Ervebo vaccine, which was developed for use against the more common Zaire strain.

Its effectiveness against the current Ebola strain caused by the Bundibugyo virus will be monitored in 20,000 recipients for up to one year.

Clinical trials are ongoing to find a licensed vaccine for the latest outbreak, which has no licensed vaccine or proven treatment.

“We don’t know to what degree it might be effective against the Bundibugyo strain,” Steve Ahuka, a Congolese official who is part of the health task force against the Ebola outbreak, said.

Dr Jeannot Elua said at a health facility in Bunia the vaccine was “beneficial”.

“We healthcare workers don’t really have a choice. We are going to receive it,” he told the Associated Press news agency. “Some people here had already received the previous vaccine. I received it myself, because it was mandatory.”

WHO experts have said that early data on the Ervebo vaccine, notably from animal trials, suggested it could offer some protection in the current outbreak.

The virus has killed at least 3,639 and infected some 7,541 people since May. Some 1,823 people have recovered, according to the latest figures from local authorities.

The WHO said in August that 70,000 doses of Ervebo were approved for use in the DRC.

The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use programme, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use.

While WHO officials have cited “encouraging signs” that transmission may be slowing, MSF warned on Friday that there is no clear evidence the epidemic is coming under control.
sources.headline: DR Congo rolls out Ebola vaccine for health workers as death toll rises

stories.headline: Millions lose power as Cuba suffers its seventh major blackout of the year

sources.body:
Millions in Cuba were left without power on Friday as the country was plunged into yet another major blackout.

The country's entire electricity grid suffered "total disconnection" that triggered a nationwide outage, Cuba's energy ministry said.

Power was restored to some priority areas by late evening, including those near hospitals and water pumping stations in the capital Havana, grid operator UNE said.

It is at least the sixth partial or total blackout to hit Cuba this year, where ageing electricity infrastructure and chronic fuel shortages have been placed under further strain by a US blockade on oil shipments to the communist-run nation.

UNE said the outage started just before 14:00 local time on Friday (18:00 GMT) due to a transmission fault coupled with poor weather conditions in central Cuba.

Protocols to begin the "gradual restoration" of power were activated, the operator's national load dispatch director Felix Estrada said, with the process ongoing on Saturday.

Cuba relies heavily on fuel imports, meaning tight US sanctions and an oil blockade since the start of the year have exacerbated existing shortages.

Food and medicine have also become more scarce, with hospitals struggling to function normally and schools and government offices having to close.

"Lately, it's becoming a habit," Havana resident Frank Lorenzo told news agency Reuters on Friday.

"Before it happened less frequently - once a month… just yesterday we were 24 hours without electricity, they turned it on for just an hour and it went down again."

"It's one thing after another: no water, no gas for cooking, no electricity," 36-year-old schoolteacher Lidia Fernandez told news agency AFP. "Honestly, I don't know how we haven't gone crazy."

Francisco Rodriguez, 78, said his home had already gone without power for 28 hours on Friday and feared he would not have light "for several days".

The repeated blackouts have prompted rare protests in Cuba, where unauthorised demonstrations are illegal and those who defy the ban risk being jailed.

Havana has blamed its fuel crisis on the Trump administration and denounced all of its sanctions - including a new round announced in August - which are part of a wider pressure campaign against the Caribbean island's leadership.

Cuba's regional ally Venezuela was believed to have sent it around 35,000 barrels of oil a day - about half of its oil needs - until Venezuela's own supplies were cut off following the US seizure of its President Nicolás Maduro in January.

US President Donald Trump has threatened tariffs on countries shipping oil to Havana, and a number of such shipments have been seized by the US.

Washington meanwhile attributes Cuba's energy crisis to poor internal management and has accused it of posing a "national security threat". Trump has openly discussed toppling its leadership, including threatening a "friendly takeover" in March this year.
sources.headline: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout

sources.body: Cuba was plunged into its seventh massive blackout of the year on Friday. The island of over nine million people endures constant power cuts due to the poor state of its aging thermoelectric plants – but the situation has worsened significantly since January, when Washington imposed a de facto energy blockade on the island. Story by Shirli Sitbon.
sources.headline: Millions without power in Cuba as electrical grid collapses again

stories.headline: Trump bars CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from the White House after calling their coverage 'fake news'

sources.body:
Politico, CNN and MS NOW journalists have been denied access to the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he was banning the outlets.

An MS NOW reporter and a photographer tried entering the White House grounds on Saturday morning, but their badges would not scan and an officer confiscated them, the outlet reported.

Both CNN and Politico also said Saturday morning that their reporters were denied access and had their badges seized.

Trump said on Friday he was barring all three major US media outlets from the White House, accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

"The officer asked me to hand over my badge. He said that it was disabled," MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner said. "I asked why I was not able to get inside. He said it was above him."

Gardner added that while her and her colleague's badges were disabled, an MS NOW producer was still able to scan her badge to get in, though she was not given an explanation as to why the producer's badge still worked.

CNN reporter Betsy Klein said a Secret Service agent told her her badge had been deactivated.

Later on Saturday morning, Politico said its reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry and Secret Service revoked her pass.

All three outlets have spoken out against the decision, accusing Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

An MS NOW spokesperson said in a statement that the White House "belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars".

MS NOW said it "intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy".

Politico Editor-in-Chief Jonathan Greenberger said in an internal email, shared in the outlet's Playbook newsletter, that the company stands by its reporters and will "vigorously defend" their First Amendment rights.

And CNN said, "we have a right under the US Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right".

In his announcement, Trump did not mention specific stories or reporting from the three outlets that prompted the move, but later said "it's really just cumulative stories over the last few years".

Trump added that there "may be others to join them", but has not given a directive banning additional news outlets. When later asked by a reporter what he meant by others to come, Trump responded: "Others to come in terms of fake news? Well, you know, the New York Times is fake news, the Washington Post is fake news."

The White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) - the independent, non-profit group that represents journalists who cover the US presidency - called on the administration "to immediately restore" access to the journalists and accused it of violating the First Amendment.

"The implications extend beyond these organizations: a standard used to exclude one news outlet because of its coverage could be applied to any outlet in the future," said WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich, who works for Fox News.

stories.headline: US gubernatorial candidates call for state-level AI safeguards amid federal inaction

sources.body: Gubernatorial candidates across the country are racing to stake out positions on AI as the battle over regulating the technology intensifies. They’re watching as sitting governors of both parties turn the rapidly evolving technology into a political priority, from Gavin Newsom in California to Ron DeSantis in Florida and Kathy Hochul in New York . Now they’re starting to join the chorus, calling for more state-based action to put guardrails on AI — even if they don’t know what that would look like yet. POLITICO reached out to more than 18 Republican and Democratic gubernatorial candidates on their plans and received responses from eight. Nearly all said they want states to take the lead on AI, signaling a frustration with Washington’s inaction and acknowledgement that — if they eventually secure the governor’s mansion — they can’t dismiss the growing warnings. Candidates said they were motivated by different concerns including fraud, job displacement and children’s safety. Their lack of detail on just how to address AI also reveals a tricky pivot these gubernatorial candidates are facing: To date, much of their campaign messaging on AI or the technology race with China has focused on data centers’ impact on energy prices. Now, with less than six weeks until Election Day, they’re attempting to talk about AI in a more existential — and more far-reaching — manner. "The federal government has failed to lead on this issue, and we cannot trust the billionaires profiting off of AI to self-regulate,” said Gina Hinojosa, Texas’ Democratic nominee for governor, in a statement. “State government has the most direct impact on our day-to-day lives, and at a time when Texans are more uncertain and concerned about AI than ever, it’s critical that we put the needs of Texans before corporate profits.” (GOP Gov. Greg Abbott, Hinojosa’s opponent, did not respond to a list of questions.) Former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who’s heavily favored to succeed Newsom in California, is in conversations with tech industry leaders and economists on the path forward. He will “work to set firm guardrails to prevent the threat of real harms to workers, to children, to our privacy rights, to public safety,” spokesperson Jonathan Underland said in a statement. “California is the birthplace of modern AI, and California will lead the way in making it safe.” Becerra’s longshot Republican opponent, Steve Hilton, told POLITICO that there’s a place for narrow regulation on AI — even though he thinks some of the warnings are overblown and “preposterous.” “California should lead on this because we are leading on the technology, and therefore we should lead on the regulation,” Hilton said. “I would prefer to see both the Congress and politicians in other states back off and stop talking about something they don't understand.” Recent warnings from top AI leaders about the technology’s potential apocalyptic trajectory roiled Democrats and Republicans both in Washington and on the campaign trail. According to a new POLITICO Poll, a majority of voters now think that AI poses an existential threat to humanity and a plurality want to see a pause in development of advanced models. “There is a lot of education that's needed here, and people are navigating an issue that they weren't even really thinking about six months ago beyond the beyond ‘Should we have data centers’?” said Alyssa Cass, a Democratic strategist who has worked with Alex Bores, a New York state lawmaker who gained national attention in his failed campaign for Congress for opposition to unchecked AI. “They're talking about it,” she added. “That's a meaningful difference.” The National Governors Association, which convened a working group on AI’s impact on the workforce earlier this year, plans to release a policy roadmap for governors in November on how states can take action. "We have 39 gubernatorial elections happening in November, and at least 21 new governors will be sworn in in January,” said Sophia Yager, the NGA’s policy director for workforce development and economic policy. “So we wanted to have a resource available not only for incumbent governors who are thinking and working on this issue, but for all of the new governors coming in, wanting to have something available for them from the jump in November." So far, Democrats have taken the sharpest aim at the Republican-controlled federal government for its inaction on establishing safeguards against AI. “While regulation is strongest and most effective at the federal level, President [Donald] Trump dismisses the need for even the most basic guardrails, and we know it can take time for Congress to act,” said Federico Araujo, a spokesperson for Oregon’s Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek, who’s locked in a tightening battle for reelection. “States, in the meantime, must act with more urgency and do everything possible to manage how AI impacts our economies, energy prices and natural resources.” David Crowley, the Democratic nominee in Wisconsin, told POLITICO in a statement that AI safety is “an issue Wisconsin can address” but “we need strong leadership and partners in Washington who are looking out for us at home.” Still, he didn’t offer specifics, and much of his battle with GOP nominee Tom Tiffany — and even the Democratic primary — has been focused on data centers’ proliferation in Wisconsin . Tiffany did not respond to a request for comment. The calls for action on state-based regulation have not been limited to Democrats alone. Republicans — including some Trump allies — signaled a willingness to create safe buffers for the technology at the state level, following the lead of governors like DeSantis and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox , who have long advocated for states’ abilities to install guardrails amid federal inaction. “States should have a say in how AI is regulated,” said Dan Capodilupo, spokesperson for Iowa GOP gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn. “Zach is committed to protecting states rights.” State Auditor Rob Sand, his Democratic opponent, did not respond to a request for comment. In Georgia, Garrison Douglas, a spokesperson for GOP nominee Rick Jackson, stopped short of calling for local regulations but said that the health care executive “supports efforts to ensure that new models are tested for risks and that safety standards are established. He added that Jackson is “committed” to working with the state legislature on protecting consumers from AI-driven scams. Georgia’s Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms did not respond to a request for comment. Trump has labeled concerns about AI’s existential threat a “HOAX” and derided efforts to regulate the technology, and his White House has pushed preemption of state-level regulation. In February, the White House urged Utah legislators to abandon an AI transparency bill ; the administration has similarly gone after state-level legislation in Colorado and in California. A POLITICO review of state-level legislation found 18 laws in 13 states, led by both Republicans and Democrats, that contradict the White House’s preemption framework. These candidates’ calls for state-based action mirror some early actions that both red and blue state executives are taking from their statehouse perches, explicitly defying Trump’s hands-off approach to regulating the nascent but powerful industry. This week, Cox urged Washington to “establish a consistent national framework for the development of frontier AI,” and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, in a speech at an AI-focused conference in Pittsburgh, called for the “federal government to step up and regulate the AI industry just like they do for nearly every other industry that significantly impacts our lives.” Shapiro — who’s up for reelection in the battleground state this year and is considered a 2028 presidential contender — outlined what he sees as the stakes of slow-walking protective measures. “By the time Congress comes back into session after the election, we could be dealing with a whole new generation of generative AI, and more scary examples of AI agents going rogue,” he said. Lisa Kashinsky contributed to this report.
sources.headline: Without federal action, candidates for governor see an opening on AI

stories.headline: Trump's plan for tariff-free beef imports creates an election-year problem for farm-state Republicans

sources.body: Farm-state Republicans don’t support President Donald Trump’s move to import cheap beef — but they’re still getting grilled for it. Trump’s plan to combat sky-high beef prices by introducing discounted, tariff-free foreign beef has been widely condemned by ag-state Republicans who are concerned it will undercut the domestic beef industry and hurt ranchers, a normally reliable constituency. And their opponents see an opening to paint Republicans as unconcerned about voters’ pocketbook concerns. “Our ranchers and our farmers keep getting kicked in the teeth, and we have politicians that keep telling us that everything's great, that we’re the hottest country,” Dan Osborn, an independent running for Senate in Nebraska, said in an interview. “And to be quite frank, I'm pretty pissed off about it.” Osborn’s state is one of the top four top cattle-producing states — along with Texas, Kansas and Iowa — all of which have more-competitive-than-expected Senate races this cycle. And Trump’s controversial plan to remove tariffs from 300,000 metric tons of imported beef, sold at 25 percent below current market prices, is doing Republicans no favors. Osborn’s campaign went on air with a pun-filled ad this week in which he says the import plan is “selling out American farmers and ranchers,” and blasts Congress for being “too chicken to stand up to the corporations who bought them off.” The campaign says it plans to spend at least six figures airing the spot. It’s the first major spending from a campaign focused on the beef import plan. But it plays into a larger economic argument Democrats are pushing to break through with farmers and ranchers: Trump and Republicans have turned their backs on rural America, as a worsening farm crisis and spiking fuel and fertilizer prices pinch agricultural communities. “It’s part of a wider frustration,” said an adviser to one of the farm-state GOP senators, granted anonymity to speak openly. “I don’t think it sways anyone’s vote, but it isn’t a great look. … It isn’t fun for me to read the headline. It’s frustrating.” Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Osborn’s opponent, said in a statement he has a record of standing for his state’s agriculture community, “no matter who is president — from fighting Biden’s 30x30 plan to opposing this beef import plan.” “Ranchers know the difference between a senator who delivers and a candidate reading a script his socialist ad agency wrote,” Ricketts said. Farm-state Democrats and independents believe beef imports provide a window to speak to rural voters who have skewed red for decades but suddenly look more competitive amid Trump’s plunging political standing. A strategist working on Osborn’s campaign, granted anonymity to discuss strategy, said Osborn’s ad “codes as non-partisan in a way that running ads about taxes or healthcare doesn’t.” Trump’s overall unpopularity is hurting Republicans across the map, but this policy could be especially problematic in a quartet of once-sleeper Senate races that could hand Democrats control of the upper chamber. Spokespeople for the GOP nominees in Iowa and Kansas declined to discuss the issue, pointing to their candidates’ statements in August, when Trump’s plan was announced: Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) called Trump’s plan a “bad idea,” while Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) said the priority should be growing the U.S. cattle herd, “not flooding the market with imports.” Last week, during a debate at the Kansas State Fair, Democratic nominee Adam Hamilton slammed the import plan as “a slap in the face of all of our cattle ranchers,” earning a raucous response from fair-goers, and hit Marshall for “tepidly respond[ing] to it as opposed to shouting like hell that this is not okay.” In Iowa’s agriculture-heavy first district, Democrats have been on the air since June with an ad hammering Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks for record-high beef prices” and other cost-of-living increases under the Trump administration. The Republicans who were already getting hammered for high prices before now are now hobbled by a proposed remedy — one that has infuriated their own base. When asked how Republicans should message the beef plan back home, Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.), chair of the Senate Agriculture Committee, acknowledged there’s “certainly a lot of concern amongst our cattle producers.” “I think they understand what's going on. They're just not pleased with it,” Boozman said. “We're in contact with the administration, a lot of members are in contact, helping them understand the unintended consequences of it. We'd like to lower prices, but again, we don't want the unintended consequence of lowering cattle futures significantly.” That leaves ranchers worried that the import plan will undercut their struggling industry. “President Trump wants to lower the price of beef, I think that's where it's coming from,” said Ben Menges, a cattle rancher in Arizona’s battleground 6th District. “The best way that President Trump can do that is by lowering the cost of fuel, not by importing a bunch of beef.” Some Republicans have looked to turn the conversation into a culture war issue — hitting their opponents for past stances on meat consumption or veganism . Vice President JD Vance, during a visit to Iowa Friday — which Hinson did not attend — slammed Hamilton, the pastor-turned-Democratic nominee for Senate in Kansas, for having a “kind of a ‘gee whiz, I'm a nice pastor’ vibe” who tells his congregation to “repent for their white privilege while eating beef.” It’s an attack Marshall made at last week’s debate, hitting Hamilton for a sermon he delivered on climate change and the impact of meat consumption. “I think the senator needs to repent for not standing up for the beef industry,” responded Hamilton.

sources.headline: El mapa de Ceuta 50 días después de la entrada: más de 10.000 migrantes entre centros y asentamientos informales

sources.body:
En Ceuta, alrededor de 8.300 migrantes están alojados en diferentes centros habilitados, aunque se calcula que más de 4.000 permanecen en las calles. Este domingo es el segundo día en el puerto con el campamento de acogida activo para 1.700 personas. La intención es poder ampliar las plazas para lo que ya trabajan operarios en la zona.

Aunque solo es para adultos, lo cierto es que permanecen algunos jóvenes que explican que son menores de edad, pero que aún no han pasado el proceso de identificación. Es el caso de Zaid, que ahora tiene 17 años. Si se confirma que es menor tendrá que pasar por un recurso específico y quedar bajo la tutela de Ceuta. El Gobierno cifra en 2.048 el número de menores ya identificados y calcula que quedan entre 700 y 1.000.

El centro de acogida del puerto continúa en el centro de la polémica. La Audiencia Nacional ha pedido al Gobierno los expedientes del campamento ante el recurso presentado por el sindicato policial SUP, que denunció la instalación por motivos de seguridad.

Mientras, en las playas sigue habiendo campamentos improvisados. La del Trampolín vuelve a estar totalmente ocupada pese a la entrada en funcionamiento del centro de acogida temporal de migrantes del puerto. "Es una oportunidad de vivir mejor, de tener un trabajo que sea bueno, de ayudar", explica uno de los migrantes.

Una acampada diferente se ha instalado en la Plaza de los Reyes, frente a la delegación del Gobierno. Sus habitantes son vecinos de Ceuta que vuelven a exigir soluciones por la crisis migratoria . "No podemos normalizar lo que no es normal; aquí estamos para pedir, a todas las administraciones, que cumplan con su responsabilidad", protestan.

A esta situación hay que añadir las denuncias de algunos menores migrantes sobre supuestas vejaciones y amenazas sufridas en centros de acogida. "Amenazas de violencia sexual por parte de guardias de seguridad; también están amenazadas por ciertas educadoras con que no se va a procesar su documentación; han dormido maniatadas noches enteras dentro de baños , como forma de castigo", explica al Canal 24 Horas una de las abogadas.

Las denuncias son ya investigadas por la Fiscalía, aunque, mientras tanto, algunos de esos menores prefieren vivir en la calle.

El vicepresidente primero y ministro de Economía, Comercio y Empresa, Carlos Cuerpo, ha exigido "lealtad" a Marruecos, en una entrevista a RTVE. Además, ha defendido los 309 millones de euros en ayudas para Ceuta y ha destacado que la población "necesita tener un horizonte de esperanza".

"La inmigración y la seguridad es un elemento de primer orden de política doméstica en todos los países de la Unión Europea y hay que incorporar a Ceuta y Melilla a todos los mecanismos que tienen que ver con la seguridad, con el refuerzo fronterizo... y luego, por supuesto, la colaboración con Marruecos, una colaboración que tiene que ser leal, y hay que exigir esa lealtad", ha declarado este sábado en una entrevista para el programa 'Informe Semanal'.

Así, el titular del ramo ha aprovechado la ocasión para mandar un mensaje de "responsabilidad a todos los que tienen algún papel en la resolución de esta crisis". "El miedo es muy difícil de combatir, y es cierto que se puede alimentar con discursos falsos o interesados", ha añadido.

Hasta ahora, todavía se trata de niños y adolescentes que habían entrado en la ciudad autónoma antes del cruce masivo del 30 y 31 de julio, porque la tramitación de los expedientes requiere de tiempo. Pero las mismas fuentes avanzan que algunos de los procesos que afectan a los llegados en la crisis están en marcha y siguen los mismos trámites, por lo <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-15/el-gobierno-preve-reubicar-a-los-menores-irregulares-en-ceuta-en-un-plazo-minimo-de-dos-meses-si-continua-el-bloqueo-del-pp.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-15/el-gobierno-preve-reubicar-a-los-menores-irregulares-en-ceuta-en-un-plazo-minimo-de-dos-meses-si-continua-el-bloqueo-del-pp.html">que continuarán similares cauces en las próximas semanas.</a> Madrid, Murcia y Galicia (del PP) también están recibiendo estos menores, así como Castilla-La Mancha (del PSOE). </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-09-19/comunidades-gobernadas-por-pp-y-vox-siguen-acogiendo-a-menores-migrantes-que-llegaron-a-ceuta-antes-de-la-crisis.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

stories.headline: Spain's National Court requests government records on the migrant camp at Ceuta's port

sources.body:
La Audiencia Nacional ha pedido al Ministerio de Transportes que le haga llegar los expedientes administrativos sobre el campamento de migrantes habilitado en el puerto de Ceuta para estudiar el recurso del sindicato policial SUP contra esta instalación por motivos de seguridad, que ha sido admitido a trámite.

Lo hace en el decreto de admisión a trámite del recurso, al que ha tenido acceso RTVE.es, en el que la Sala de lo Contencioso Administrativo da al Ejecutivo un plazo improrrogable de veinte días para remitirle la documentación.

Además, precisa que, en el caso de que haya documentos declarados confidenciales , estos deben quedar en depósito de la Administración, aunque "a plena disposición del tribunal".

Esta admisión a trámite, que no prejuzga el fondo del recurso, llega después de que la Audiencia Nacional decidiese el pasado jueves rechazar la medida cautelarísima solicitada por el sindicato policial de frenar la habilitación del espacio portuario para alojar a los migrantes llegados a la ciudad autónoma durante la crisis migratoria.

Tras la denegación de esta medida cautelar y mientras la Sala de lo Contencioso Administrativo estudia el fondo del recurso, el Gobierno ha seguido adelante con su plan para alojar a los migrantes y trasladó este viernes a 1.700 personas desde las playas de Benítez y El Trampolín al nuevo centro temporal.

En un comunicado, el sindicato policial SUP ha defendido su tesis de los riesgos de seguridad que puede acarrear este dispositivo de acogida y ha recordado que la Autoridad Portuaria de Ceuta inicialmente rechazó esta ubicación por considerarla incompatible con la normal explotación del puerto, aunque posteriormente Puertos del Estado informó favorablemente por razones de interés general.

Ahora que el campamento está operativo, el SUP ha asegurado que exigirá "conocer y fiscalizar" las evaluaciones de riesgos, protocolos, efectivos y medios previstos para garantizar la seguridad de los policías destinados en "un entorno especialmente sensible".

"Nuestra obligación como sindicato no es esperar a que ocurra un incidente para lamentarlo, sino anticiparnos al riesgo y proteger a nuestros compañeros", han remarcado en la nota remitida.

Contra la presente resolución cabe interponer recurso de reposición en el plazo de cinco días a contar desde el siguiente al de su notificación.

sources.body: Barcelona tindrà una xarxa de comerços assequibles semblant als supermercats públics que l’alcalde de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani , impulsarà a la ciutat estatunidenca a partir de l’any que ve. El projecte començarà amb una prova pilot al barri de la Marina i l’objectiu és poder oferir als veïns del barri “ producte fresc assequible “. “Hi ha molts punts de coincidència” Ho ha anunciat l’alcalde de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, després de reunir-se amb Mamdani a Nova York. “Hi ha molts punts de coincidència entre el projecte dels súpers públics de Mamdani i el nostre”, ha dit el batlle. La iniciativa barcelonina serà gestionada per una entitat del tercer sector, una ONG , en un edifici de titularitat municipal , segons ha detallat Collboni. Foto: Ajuntament de Barcelona A més, el projecte estarà també vinculat a un programa de formació professional . Collboni ha afegit que la idea de la mesura és “fer més assequible la vida de les famílies treballadores de les grans ciutats”. Barcelona i Nova York aniran intercanviant-se informació “per veure com evolucionen les experiències”. També et pot interessar Barcelona crea un fons per comprar comerços “emblemàtics i estratègics” en risc de desaparèixer Ester Magdaleno Helena Molist Sancho 2 minuts de lectura Viatge institucional als EUA Collboni es troba de visita institucional a la capital financera dels EUA perquè assistirà a la cimera de ciutats Urban20 , que se celebra durant aquest cap de setmana. Es tracta d’un espai en què els dirigents de grans ciutats del món debatran sobre habitatge , sensellarisme , canvi climàtic i immigració . També et pot interessar Collboni es reunirà amb l’alcalde de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, en un viatge institucional als EUA Roger Torres i Liñán 1 minut de lectura Precisament, l’alcalde diu que ha traslladat a Mamdani les polítiques en habitatge que Barcelona ha aplicat fins ara, com la regulació dels preus dels lloguers o la decisió d’ eliminar tots els pisos turístics a partir del 2028. Decisions, ha dit l’alcalde, que “estan contribuint a fer més assequible l’habitatge a la ciutat progressivament”.
sources.headline: Barcelona tindrà una xarxa de comerços assequibles semblant als supermercats públics de Nova York

sources.body:
L'alcalde de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, està de viatge oficial a Nova York per assistir a la trobada internacional Urban20, en què participen una quarantena de ciutats d'arreu del món.

Abans de la seva intervenció en aquesta cimera, Collboni s'ha trobat aquest dissabte amb l'alcalde de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, "per compartir visions i projectes de les seves respectives ciutats", segons ha informat en un comunicat el consistori barceloní. Els dos batlles han parlat de polítiques d'habitatges, cooperació internacional entre grans nuclis urbans, resiliència climàtica i ajudes públiques en la distribució d'aliments.

Entre els projectes compartits hi ha la idea de crear "una xarxa de comerços assequibles" a Barcelona, similar a la que s'està fent a Nova York, "per garantir que les famílies treballadores i de classes mitjanes" puguin accedir als béns bàsics de primera necessitat. El primer d'aquests comerços s'obrirà al districte de Sants Montjuïc, a finals del 2027 , i el gestionarà una entitat del tercer sector, segons ha explicat Collboni.

Estem preparant l'aterratge del primer pla pilot al barri de la Marina, un projecte que estarà gestionat per una ONG.

L'entitat que se n'encarregui oferirà productes assequibles a la població que ho necessiti. Treballarà des d'un edifici municipal en un projecte que vincularà alimentació assequible amb comerç de barri, un programa de formació professional i inserció laboral en oficis com la fruiteria, la peixateria, la carnisseria, la xarcuteria, la reposició i l'atenció al client.

Els establiments se situaran en plantes baixes de titularitat municipal i volen garantir una oferta alimentària de qualitat i assequible en zones en transformació o amb poc comerç d'alimentació tradicional. L'alcalde ha insistit que el projecte no intenta competir ni amb els mercats municipals ni amb el comerç privat, sinó cobrir un buit en barris de nova creació o vulnerables "on falten alguns béns de primera necessitat".

La idea s'emmiralla en la proposta anunciada fa uns mesos per l'alcalde de Nova York, Zohran Mamdani, que s'ha compromès a obrir cinc supermercats públics municipals per fer front a l'escalada de preus dels aliments bàsics, que en aquesta ciutat s'han enfilat un 56% en l'última dècada.

En aquests supermercats, alguns aliments es podran trobar un 30% més barats . La idea de Mamdani és preparar un cistell bàsic de productes frescos com peix, carn, làctics o verdures dirigit a tots els ciutadans, independentment dels ingressos que tinguin, perquè no hagin d'estalviar en menjar per arribar a final de mes.

Els càlculs de l'Ajuntament de Nova York és que la mesura permeti a cada família estalviar uns 90 dòlars mensuals , el que equivaldria a uns 1.000 dòlars l'any.

Segons fonts de l'Ajuntament de Barcelona, Collboni i Mamdani també han coincidit en la necessitat que les grans ciutats del món estiguin connectades en xarxa, "mantinguin la multilateralitat i aprenguin les unes de les altres" per assumir conjuntament els grans reptes que afronten en aquests moments. Sobretot, ha dit Collboni, "en un moment en què les democràcies en molts països estan amenaçades i on el multilateralisme és atacat i menystingut". I entre aquests grans reptes han destacat fer front a la crisi de l'habitatge i aconseguir que en aquests nuclis urbans hi hagi vivendes assequibles per als seus residents.
sources.headline: Collboni anuncia un supermercat assequible a Barcelona a finals del 2027 semblant als de Nova York

sources.body: (ACN) La responsable de compliment d’ERC, Mireia Ingla, ha presentat aquest dissabte al Consell Nacional del partit les conclusions de la comissió de garanties sobre l’afer dels cartells que vinculaven Ernest Maragall i el seu germà Pasqual amb l’Alzheimer . sources.headline: ERC tanca l’expedient pel cas dels cartells dels Maragall i l’Alzheimer i demana “perdó”

sources.body:
Després de tres anys , la Comissió de Garanties d'Esquerra Republicana ha presentat les conclusions de la investigació oberta pels cartells que van aparèixer a diverses seus d'ERC en què denigraven els germans Maragall , durant la campanya de les municipals del 2023. Als cartells hi havia la imatge d'Ernest i Pasqual Maragall amb el lema "Fora l'Alzheimer de Barcelona".

Els responsables d'aquesta polèmica campanya són els exdirigents del partit Sergi Sabrià i Marc Colomer , que van ocupar la vicesecretaria general de Comunicació d'ERC entre el 2016 i el 2023, segons l'informe. El partit els atribueix a tots dos una infracció greu com a màxims responsables d'aquesta campanya denigrant, però no els obre cap expedient disciplinari perquè ja no són militants d'Esquerra Republicana.

L'informe, presentat aquest dissabte en el marc del Consell Nacional del partit, rebaixa la responsabilitat de l'exdirector de Comunicació d'ERC Tolo Moya i d'un militant de l'Anoia que va penjar els cartells, en considerar que obeïen ordres.

El juliol del 2024, el partit va obrir un expedient a tots quatre militants , després de reconèixer que els cartells despectius havien sortit de les seves files. En un primer moment, els Mossos havien detingut tres joves, a qui van acusar d'un delicte d'odi per penjar-los.

Els cartells van aparèixer durant la campanya de les últimes eleccions municipals del 28 de maig del 2023. S'hi podia llegir el missatge "Fora l'Alzheimer de Barcelona", darrere la imatge de l'aleshores alcaldable d'ERC a Barcelona, Ernest Maragall, i la del seu germà i expresident de la Generalitat, Pasqual Maragall, que té aquesta malaltia.

L'informe també responsabilitza Sergi Sabrià del ninot amb la imatge del líder d'ERC Oriol Junqueras penjant d'un pont a Sant Vicenç dels Horts, al Baix Llobregat, abans de les eleccions europees del 2019. I considera que va ser una altra acció de falsa bandera promoguda per Sabrià, aleshores responsable de Comunicació del partit.

Després de la presentació de l'informe, el secretari adjunt d'ERC, Oriol López, ha demanat perdó "pel mal fet" , especialment a la família de Pasqual i Ernest Maragall, així com a la militància de Barcelona i al conjunt de la formació.

López ha dit que miraran de reparar el mal fet, s'ha compromès a garantir que no torni a passar res semblant i ha donat el cas per tancat. Un cas del qual, ha assegurat, n'han tret lliçons per garantir "la transparència" i "traçabilitat" de les decisions i el control dels recursos per "impossibilitar qualsevol estructura informal o paral·lela".

sources.body: La  previsió  del temps  per a aquest diumenge, 20 de setembre, indica un dia radiant i amb temperatures encara més altes. La calor encara anirà a més a principis de setmana, quan es podran superar amb escreix els 30 ºC. Previsió horària per a Barcelona : 6 h: nit tropical al centre 9 h: bones condicions per a la cursa de la Mercè 12 h: sense núvols 15 h: a tocar dels 30 ºC 18 h: tarda serena 21 h: nit més càlida També et pot interessar L’aigua del mar supera encara les mitjanes de l’estiu i marca un altre rècord al setembre Marcos Amores Sánchez 3 minuts de lectura Gairebé sense núvols El sol s’imposarà de manera clara a Barcelona i la resta de Catalunya. Apareixeran alguns núvols prims passatgers concentrats a la tarda i especialment a l’interior i Pirineus. Anecdòtics. Temperatures una mica més altes , amb màximes que podran superar puntualment els 30 ºC al prelitoral i que s’acostaran a aquesta marca a Barcelona. Diumenge de calor intensa a ponent i l’interior de la vall de l’Ebre, on alguna raconada pot tocar els 33 ºC. També et pot interessar Nits tropicals i tòrrides a Barcelona: quantes n’hem tingut ja? | GRÀFICS Manel Cascante Torrella Marcos Amores Sánchez Oriol Rodríguez Ballester 2 minuts de lectura Les temperatures més altes, en funció del vent La setmana començarà amb un pic de calor com a conseqüència de l’entrada del vent de garbí aquest dilluns. Sol i calor per començar la setmana, amb màximes de més de 30 ºC a Barcelona i bona part de la resta de la regió metropolitana. El vent girarà dimarts, de recorregut marítim i ens tornarà a la casella de sortida. La calor continuarà, però serà menys intensa. Dimecres arribarà oficialment la tardor, però l’estiu té corda per dies.
